title: NPRI Reporting for Oil and Gas in Canada
summary: Learn how Canadian oil and gas facilities prepare NPRI reports, which pollutants and emissions sources to consider, and what operating data supports reporting.
body_markdown:
Canadian oil and gas operators use fuel consumption, flared and vented gas volumes, equipment inventories, and production records to prepare their annual National Pollutant Release Inventory (NPRI) reports. These records help quantify releases of pollutants such as nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide, volatile organic compounds, and benzene. Reporting requirements vary by facility, determining which pollutants and emissions sources must be included. The appropriate quantification methods depend on the source and the data available.


## What does NPRI reporting cover?


The NPRI is Canada’s public inventory of pollutant releases, disposals, and transfers for recycling. Owners and operators that meet the reporting requirements submit the year’s information to Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) through the online reporting system. Depending on the substance and the criteria that apply, that submission can include releases to air, water, and land, as well as disposals and off-site transfers for recycling.


The[notice published on 8 March 2025](https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-03-08/html/sup1-eng.html) sets the substance list for the 2025, 2026, and 2027 reporting years.[ECCC’s oil and gas reporting guide](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-pollutant-release-inventory/report/sector-specific-tools-calculate-emissions/oil-gas-guide.html) focuses primarily on criteria air contaminants and individual volatile organic compounds. Gas processing plants and refineries may also have to report other listed substances, depending on their operations and the criteria that apply. The[Guide for reporting to the NPRI for 2025 to 2027](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-pollutant-release-inventory/report/reporting-guide.html) sets out the requirements for each substance category.


Facilities with reporting obligations beyond air emissions may also rely on wastewater monitoring results, waste characterization data, and disposal or recycling records.


## Which oil and gas facilities need to report to the NPRI?


NPRI reporting requirements depend on facility type, employee hours, operating activities, and the substance-specific criteria in the[current Canada Gazette notice](https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-03-08/html/sup1-eng.html) . If the only activities during the year are exploration for oil or gas, or the drilling of oil or gas wells, that notice does not apply. Applicability must be assessed separately for each calendar year.


For certain oil and gas extraction facilities below the employee-hour threshold, other than compressor stations and oil sands extraction, emissions from stationary combustion equipment determine whether a reporting threshold is met. Meeting the threshold for one criteria air contaminant then requires reporting of all seven criteria air contaminants and of benzene, including releases from storage tanks, equipment leaks, flaring, and venting. Those substances are still included when there is no on-site release. Other individual VOCs may also need to be reported where their applicable reporting thresholds are met.


Facilities that meet the employee-hour threshold, or that carry out certain specified activities regardless of employee hours, have to consider the criteria for each listed substance. Large gas plants, refineries, oil sands operations, and qualifying terminal operations may be in that group. Pipeline installations and certain compressor stations are subject to reporting requirements focused on releases from stationary combustion equipment. A compressor station that forms part of a larger contiguous facility may be subject to broader reporting requirements.


Certain light and medium crude oil batteries report total volatile organic compounds and benzene from storage tanks, whether or not those substances meet the release thresholds that apply at other facilities. If the tanks have no release, both substances are still reported.[ECCC’s oil and gas reporting guide](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-pollutant-release-inventory/report/sector-specific-tools-calculate-emissions/oil-gas-guide.html) explains which requirements apply to a particular facility.


If a facility reported to the NPRI in the previous year but no longer meets any reporting criteria, the owner or operator must notify ECCC by the reporting deadline and explain why. Operators should confirm their regulatory facility boundaries, which may differ from how wells and equipment are grouped in operational systems.


## Which pollutants and emissions sources are relevant to NPRI reporting?


The seven criteria air contaminants in the oil and gas guidance are nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), total volatile organic compounds (VOCs), total particulate matter, PM₁₀, and PM₂.₅. Benzene is an individual VOC that may need to be reported separately under the applicable NPRI requirements. Its emissions can also contribute to the reported total VOC quantity. Sulphur dioxide from stationary combustion depends on the sulphur in the fuel.


The operating data needed to quantify these pollutants varies by emissions source. The following table identifies common oil and gas emissions sources, the operating records used to quantify releases, and examples of the associated pollutants.

Leak detection surveys identify leaking equipment, but[quantifying fugitive emissions](https://blog.validere.com/fugitive-emissions-oil-and-gas) also requires an appropriate estimation method.


## How are emissions quantified for NPRI reporting?


Facilities must use monitoring or measurement data already required under federal or provincial legislation or a municipal bylaw. Where no such measurement requirement applies, the[2025 to 2027 reporting guide](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-pollutant-release-inventory/report/reporting-guide.html) still requires reasonable efforts to obtain the information needed for the report. Depending on the pollutant and the emissions source, that effort may include additional monitoring, source testing, or equipment specifications from a supplier.


**Emission factors.** An emission factor relates an operating activity, such as fuel consumption, to the amount of a pollutant released. For example, estimating NOₓ emissions from a compressor engine requires a factor appropriate for the engine type, the fuel, and the operating conditions. The guide warns that some published factors are out of date or underestimate the release. When fuel consumption comes from[SCADA or a historian](https://blog.validere.com/scada-data-emissions-reporting-oil-and-gas) , the measurements still have to match the equipment, the activity, and the reporting period.


**Continuous and predictive monitoring.** Continuous monitoring measures pollutant concentration and flow over time. Predictive monitoring estimates emission rates from a tested relationship with operating parameters, such as fuel use or temperature.


**Source testing.** Source testing measures pollutant concentrations in samples from sources such as stacks or wastewater discharges. Those concentrations are combined with flow data to estimate the release.


**Mass balance.** A mass balance estimates a release from the amount of a substance entering a process, leaving it, or accumulating in it. It can be particularly useful for estimating solvent losses. It is less suitable where a chemical reaction transforms the substance.


**Speciation profiles.** A speciation profile estimates the composition of a pollutant mixture, so that total VOC emissions, for example, can be split into individual compounds.


**Remote quantification.** Remote quantification uses technologies such as optical remote sensing to measure pollutants from a distance and estimate the release.


**Engineering estimates.** An engineering estimate uses equipment specifications, operating conditions, and process knowledge when the facility does not have measured data or a suitable factor.


The online reporting system records one basis of estimate for each type of release, disposal, or transfer. When more than one method contributes to a reported quantity, the operator identifies the method that accounts for the largest share. Any other method can be described in a comment.


## NPRI reporting vs. greenhouse gas reporting and Directive 060


The same operating data can support more than one Canadian reporting requirement. Natural gas consumption from a compressor engine can support NOₓ and CO calculations for the NPRI, and carbon dioxide (CO₂) calculations for Canada’s federal Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP). Where applicable, the NPRI submission must also include the facility’s GHGRP identification number.


In Alberta,[Directive 060](https://www.aer.ca/regulating-development/rules-and-directives/directives/directive-060) sets flaring, incinerating, and venting requirements for upstream petroleum wells and facilities, and for gas pipeline installations licensed by the Alberta Energy Regulator. Flared and vented gas records can support both Directive 060 reporting obligations and pollutant calculations for the NPRI, although each has distinct reporting requirements.


## What records should be kept for NPRI reporting?


Supporting records should let a reviewer trace a reported pollutant quantity back to the emissions sources, the operating data, the measurements, and the calculation method. Documenting emission factors, assumptions, reporting periods, and internal approvals also helps explain differences between reporting years. An[in-house compliance reporting program](https://blog.validere.com/in-house-compliance-reporting-program) can establish consistent procedures for reviewing, approving, and correcting those calculations before submission.


For reportable criteria air contaminants and speciated VOCs, the[8 March 2025 notice](https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-03-08/html/sup1-eng.html) requires a monthly breakdown of air releases as a percentage of the annual release, and the reasons those air releases changed from the previous year. Maintaining monthly emissions estimates alongside their supporting operating records helps explain year-over-year changes in reported releases. These may result from changes in production, equipment, operating hours, fuel composition, or calculation methods.


The certifying official electronically signs a statement that the information is true, complete, and accurate, and that the data will be made public. That official is legally responsible for the report. The environmental team’s review of the data and the calculations is separate from that statement.


Under the current NPRI notice, the owner or operator must keep copies of the information submitted and the supporting calculations, measurements, and other data for three years from the reporting deadline. Those records must be kept at the facility or at the owner or operator’s principal place of business in Canada.


## Frequently asked questions


### Do all oil and gas facilities need to report to the NPRI?


No. Reporting depends on the facility type, the employee hours, the activities, and whether a listed substance meets the criteria in the[8 March 2025 notice](https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-03-08/html/sup1-eng.html) .[ECCC’s oil and gas reporting guide](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/national-pollutant-release-inventory/report/sector-specific-tools-calculate-emissions/oil-gas-guide.html) explains which requirements apply to a specific facility.


### Is an NPRI report the same as Canada’s greenhouse gas report?


No. An NPRI report covers listed pollutant releases, disposals, and transfers for recycling. Canada’s federal Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program collects greenhouse gas emissions. Fuel consumption can support both, for example NOₓ in the NPRI report and CO₂ in the greenhouse gas report.


### When is NPRI reporting due in Canada?


Under the notice published on 8 March 2025, a report is due by 1 June of the following year. The 2026 report is due by 1 June 2027, and the 2027 report by 1 June 2028.
